title: Normalization-Free Spiking Networks with Lateral Inhibition
one_liner: Replace artificial normalization with biologically realistic inhibitory circuits that regulate how strongly neurons fire.
lead: Spiking neural networks are energy-efficient models inspired by how real brains compute: instead of always-on computations, neurons only transmit information via discrete spikes, consuming power only when they fire. But training deep ones has required artificial normalization (a math trick to keep neuron activity stable). This paper builds deep spiking networks without that trick, using the brain's own inhibitory circuits instead: excitatory neurons (the speakers) and inhibitory neurons (the silencers) work together to keep activity from exploding or dying out, just like the cortex does.

paras: In a spiking neural network, neurons fire discrete spikes (all-or-nothing events) only when their internal voltage crosses a threshold. Because power consumption in neural hardware is proportional to the number of spike events, not to the dimension of the network, spiking networks use far less energy than dense neural networks that compute on every layer for every input sample. But training deep networks of spiking neurons is hard: as signals pass through many layers, the voltage can either explode (growing so large every neuron fires constantly) or die (shrinking so all neurons stay silent). The standard fix is to add a normalization layer—a mathematical scaling step that artificially squashes the voltage back into a safe range. This works, but it does not exist in the brain.

A beginner might try training a deep spiking network layer-by-layer, assuming each layer stabilizes on its own. It breaks: as you add more layers, the dynamics of early layers feed into later ones unpredictably, and the cascade either saturates or vanishes. You are forced to choose: use artificial normalization (lose biological realism) or watch deep networks fail to train.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Instead of normalization, use two teams of neurons—excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) neurons arranged like brain cortex—to regulate activity dynamically through subtractive inhibition (cutting raw voltage) and divisive inhibition (scaling how responsive neurons are).

steps.text: Each layer has excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) neuron populations connected like cortex.

steps.b: E-I Init: balance from the start
steps.text: Initialize weights so expected excitatory input approximately equals expected inhibitory input for each E neuron.

steps.b: E-I Prop: guard the learning signal flow
steps.text: During learning, clip tiny divisive currents and scale large inhibitory learning signals to prevent numerical explosions.
Excitatory neurons spike, firing spikes; inhibitory neurons fire in response and subtract/scale excitatory voltage.
Weights learn to maintain the E-I balance while solving the task, no artificial normalization needed.

paras: The paper replaces the simple feedforward layer with an excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) circuit: each layer now contains two populations of neurons (E and I) that communicate with each other. Excitatory neurons drive activity forward; inhibitory neurons regulate how strong that activity can grow. The key is that inhibition works two ways: subtractive (directly removing voltage) and divisive (scaling the sensitivity). This replaces what normalization used to do artificially.

hidden.name: Expected net input to each excitatory neuron
paras: The paper measures a quantity that does not appear in the network output but controls whether training succeeds: the expected voltage each excitatory neuron receives after combining excitatory input (from the previous layer) and inhibitory input (from the inhibitory neurons). If this expected value is far from zero, neurons either saturate (always firing) or stay silent (never firing), and training collapses. The paper estimates this by assuming each presynaptic (input) neuron fires at an average probability (a spike rate), then computing the expected currents mathematically.

The paper uses this hidden quantity to initialize weights wisely: set the synaptic weights so that the expected excitatory current approximately equals the expected subtractive inhibitory current. This makes the expected net input near zero at initialization, putting every neuron in the sweet spot where it can both fire and silence itself based on input, because a neuron near zero voltage can respond to small increases in excitation by firing, and also quickly silence itself when inhibition kicks in—this responsive middle ground is where learning can actually happen.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger expected input current; boxes show neurons critical to E-I balance.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is: the sum of excitatory current minus inhibitory current, averaged over neurons. If it stays near zero, training stays stable.
Expected net input is E[I_EE,i] - E[I_EI,sub,i], balanced at initialization via point estimates of firing probability from the first training batch.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: Without inhibitory control, signals in a deep network amplify chaotically: layer 1 output becomes layer 2 input, which grows further in layer 3, and so on. Artificial normalization clamps this artificially. The paper instead uses biology: excitatory neurons fire and send spikes forward; inhibitory neurons simultaneously fire in response and send two kinds of inhibitory current backward into the excitatory neurons. Subtractive inhibition directly reduces the excitatory voltage (like turning down a volume knob). Divisive inhibition scales the gain of the excitatory neurons (like adjusting the sensitivity of a microphone so loud sounds do not saturate it). Together, these two inhibitory pathways regulate activity to stay in a middle zone—active but bounded.

The second key is how to initialize and train this circuit stably. Initialization is critical: if weights are random, inhibition is weak, and neurons saturate immediately (either all fire or all silent). The paper's E-I Init scheme computes the expected firing probability from data, then sets weights such that expected excitatory and expected inhibitory currents approximately cancel—neurons wake up balanced, not drowning in signal or starving. During training, E-I Prop guards the learning signal flow: tiny divisive currents (near zero) cause numerical explosions during differentiation, so they are clamped; large inhibitory learning signals also destabilize training, so they are scaled down. With these guards, learning signals flow cleanly through many layers, and the network learns end-to-end without any artificial normalization trick.

stages.s: Inhibition subtracts and scales E neurons

math.words: The subthreshold membrane potential of an excitatory neuron at the next time step is the current potential, decayed by a time constant, minus any spikes emitted, plus excitatory and inhibitory input currents.
math.equation: u_E[t+1] = (1 - 1/tau_E) * u_E[t] - theta_E * s_E[t] + I_EE[t] - I_EI[t]
symbols: membrane voltage of excitatory neuron at next time step
time constant controlling how fast voltage decays
spike output (1 if fired, 0 if silent)
excitatory input current (from previous E neurons)
inhibitory input current (from I neurons), subtractive and divisive

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose tau_E = 2.0, theta_E = 1.0, u_E starts at 0.0.
At time 0: I_EE[0] = 1.6 (excitatory input), I_EI[0] = 0.6 (inhibitory suppression).
At time 1: neuron spikes (s_E[1] = 1), so next step includes - theta_E * 1 = - 1.0.
u_E[2] = 0.5 * 1.0 - 1.0 * 1 + 1.5 - 0.5 = 0.5 (voltage resets, neuron is alive for next cycle).
Without inhibition (I_EI = 0), voltage would grow: u_E[2] = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2.0, soon saturated. Inhibition keeps it bounded.

math.note: Inhibitory current (I_EI) acts as a dynamic brake: stronger excitatory input triggers stronger inhibitory response, preventing saturation and keeping neurons in the active range even over many layers, because the inhibition automatically scales up with the excitatory signal, so no matter how strong the input gets, the net effect stays bounded instead of exploding like it would without that negative feedback.

charts.title: With artificial normalization (old way)
charts.note: Normalization works well for accuracy but adds overhead and lacks brain realism.

charts.title: With E-I circuits (this paper)
charts.note: No accuracy loss, cleaner energy profile, highly biologically plausible; normalization-free.

items.html: If you randomly initialize weights without respecting E-I balance, neurons will either saturate (fire constantly) or go silent. The E-I Init scheme prevents this by computing expected firing rates from data and setting weights to cancel expected currents.

Divisive inhibition can produce very small currents, which blow up when differentiated (the learning signal becomes huge). E-I Prop clamps near-zero values to the smallest positive value in a batch, keeping learning signals stable.

The inhibitory synaptic weights can produce disproportionately large learning signals (updates that are too big), throwing off the optimization. E-I Prop scales these learning signals down adaptively.

items.b: Done right: circuit adapts with learning.
items.html: When E-I Init and E-I Prop are applied together, the circuit self-regulates during training. Weights evolve to maintain E-I balance while solving the task, allowing stable end-to-end training through arbitrarily deep networks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a spiking network 5-10 layers deep. Train it on a simple classification task (e.g., CIFAR-10) or a neuromorphic dataset (e.g., DVS-Gesture, which records spikes directly from event cameras). Implement three variants: (1) standard feedforward SNNs with artificial batch normalization, (2) unconstrained E-I SNNs without E-I Init or E-I Prop (should fail or collapse), and (3) full E-I SNNs with both E-I Init and E-I Prop. Track the following metrics across training.
demo.metric_eq: Training stability = whether network trains to convergence without numerical errors or collapse; Forgetting = initial accuracy on first batch vs. accuracy after 50 updates (should be small); E-I balance = average absolute net input per layer at initialization (should be < 0.1).
demo.closing: The demo must show: (a) unconstrained E-I fails or trains slowly, (b) E-I Init + E-I Prop matches normalization in accuracy with no artificial tricks, and (c) E-I circuit voltage profiles stay bounded throughout training, proving that inhibition dynamically stabilizes activity without external intervention.
